passage:
At ten, Asif spent a whole Sunday afternoon spinning a wooden top on the veranda with his cousin Shalini, racing it from the tiles to the step. When his mother called him for tea he came in flushed and grinning. A boy in his class had a remote-control car; Asif barely gave it a thought.

At fifteen, Asif still had a working phone and decent marks in every subject. Then one evening he scrolled through friends' posts: a new phone with three cameras, a holiday by the sea, a cousin's certificate for topping the class. He looked at his own phone, which had been fine at breakfast, and it felt slow and old. He held his 78 percent up against a friend's 91. His sister Urmila found him staring at the ceiling. 'What's wrong?' 'Nothing changed,' he said slowly. 'I just suddenly feel like I have nothing.' Urmila raised her eyebrows. 'Same phone, same marks as last week, Asif.' He laughed, embarrassed, and put the phone face-down.

qa.q: What did Asif and Shalini do on the veranda?
qa.a: They raced a wooden top from the tiles to the step.

qa.q: What changed between Asif's contentment at ten and his restlessness at fifteen, and what stayed the same?
qa.a: At ten a wooden top and an afternoon with Shalini were enough, and he barely thought about the classmate's toy car. At fifteen, scrolling friends' posts made the same phone and marks feel like nothing, though nothing about them had changed.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling as he stared at the ceiling?
qa.a: Dissatisfied and lacking after comparing himself with friends' posts, and a little confused because nothing had really changed.

qa.q: What could Asif do to protect his contentment while scrolling?
qa.a: Notice what he already has, take breaks from the posts, and remember Urmila's point that nothing had changed. 🙂

grounding: Contentment at ten with a simple toy and its erosion at fifteen through comparison with friends' posts, with nothing real having changed.

passage:
At five, Wasim curled in his mother Maria's lap after a noisy fair, her hand moving slowly along his back. His breathing slowed to match hers, and his fingers unclenched from her dupatta. He fell asleep, heavy and warm.

At twenty-one, Wasim sat outside the seminar room before his viva, palms damp. His friend Tushar whispered, 'Are you nervous?' 'Very,' said Wasim. 'But I've revised what I can, and the rest isn't mine to decide.' He pressed his feet into the floor and let out one long breath, the way he had breathed in his mother's lap without knowing it. When the door opened he stood, heart still fast, and walked in steadily. Halfway through a hard question he paused, said, 'That's a good point; let me think,' and answered in his own time.

qa.q: Where did Wasim curl up after the fair?
qa.a: In his mother Maria's lap.

qa.q: How did the calm Wasim felt at five connect with his calm at twenty-one?
qa.a: At five his calm was borrowed from his mother's slow breathing in her lap. At twenty-one he made it himself with one long breath and by accepting that the rest was not his to decide, staying steady though his heart was still fast.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling outside the seminar room?
qa.a: Nervous, as his damp palms and the word 'Very' show, but also settled by accepting what he could not control.

qa.q: What could Tushar do to help before the viva?
qa.a: Stay beside him quietly and remind him to breathe, without adding more worry.

grounding: Serenity borrowed from a parent's calm at five becomes a practised steadiness under pressure at twenty-one, with nerves still present.

passage:
Age five: Sharmila stopped dead at the window, mouth open. A rainbow arched over the wet street. 'Why is it curved? Where does it end? Can it hear us?' Her grandmother crouched beside her without answering right away, just looking too, and Sharmila's questions came slower and softer.

Age ten: Avni lay on the terrace at night with her uncle, looking at a sky full of stars away from the city's glow. 'How many are there?' 'More than we can count.' She felt tiny, like a grain of rice, and oddly happy. She forgot about the quarrel with her friend.

Age fifteen: Rafiq waited at the bus stop in heavy rain. A stranger held an umbrella over Rafiq and an old woman until the bus came, then walked away without a word. On the ride home Rafiq kept replaying it. He stood at his gate for a while afterwards with a strange lightness in his chest, and the exam worry that had sat there all day felt smaller.

qa.q: What did Avni compare herself to under the stars?
qa.a: A grain of rice.

qa.q: How did awe differ across five, ten and fifteen?
qa.a: Sharmila's awe at a rainbow was bodily and full of questions, and her grandmother deepened it by looking too. Avni felt tiny yet happy under a sky full of stars and forgot her quarrel, and Rafiq was lifted above his exam worry by a stranger's kindness.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling at his gate?
qa.a: Lightness and gratitude, moved by the stranger's kindness so that his exam worry felt smaller.

qa.q: What could an adult do to deepen a child's awe, as Sharmila's grandmother did?
qa.a: Crouch down and look together at the wonder instead of rushing to give quick answers.

grounding: Awe at five, ten and fifteen: a rainbow, a vast starry sky, and a stranger's kindness, each lifting attention beyond self.

passage:
Age two: after the zoo outing, Binita refused the new picture book and asked for her worn blue elephant instead. She sat on the floor of her mother's room, quiet, pressed against her mother's knee. When a visiting aunt offered a clapping game, Binita's lip wobbled and she burst into tears. Her mother scooped her up. 'Enough for today.' Binita slept for two hours and woke calm.

Age fifteen: Thomas's week ran from school till two, tuition till five, cricket coaching till seven and homework until eleven. He felt flat, snapped at his little sister and lay awake with a tight stomach. His father crossed out one tuition class on the timetable and wrote 'free' in the Saturday slot. On the first Saturday Thomas stared at the ceiling and felt guilty. By the third he was drawing, and his flat mood had lifted.

Age twenty: on Sunday Ujjwal lay on his hostel bed with a book and felt his chest tighten. Shouldn't he be doing something? He opened his laptop, then closed it. 'Rest is what makes Monday's work possible,' a senior had once told him. He put the phone down, went for a long walk by the lake and realised his shoulders had dropped. He came back and slept without the usual dread.

qa.q: What did Thomas's father write in the Saturday slot?
qa.a: The word 'free'.

qa.q: How did rest matter at two, fifteen and twenty?
qa.a: At two Binita needed quiet, her toy and closeness after the outing and fell apart when pushed. At fifteen Thomas's packed timetable left him flat until a free Saturday brought back his drawing, and at twenty Ujjwal felt guilty about lying still until a lake walk showed him that rest makes later work possible.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling as he lay on the bed with a book?
qa.a: Anxious and guilty, as his tightening chest and the urge to open his laptop show.

qa.q: What did Thomas's father change, and why did it help?
qa.a: He crossed out one class and left a free slot, which gave Thomas room to recover, so his flat mood lifted.

grounding: Rest and recovery at two, fifteen and twenty: a toddler recharging, a teen with no free time, and a young adult guilty about resting.

passage:
Age two: Seema tripped on the rug and sat down hard. She looked straight at her mother, then laughed. Her mother stayed calm. 'Oops, bump. All good.' Seema's laughter turned into a little sniffle, and then she climbed up to be hugged.

Age fifteen: Swati arrived late and was called into the principal's office. As the scolding began, she laughed. The principal frowned. 'You think this is funny?' Swati's laugh cracked and her eyes stung. 'No, I'm sorry. I laugh when I'm scared.' A teacher passing the door said gently, 'Take a breath,' and the principal's voice softened.

Age twenty-five: Amandeep spilled coffee on the slides just before a client meeting and it went badly. Afterwards, joking to a friend, Amandeep said, 'Well, that went well. I'm now a professional at ruining slides.' The friend did not laugh. 'Are you actually okay?' Amandeep paused. 'Not really. I was up until three preparing.'

qa.q: What did Seema's mother say after the bump?
qa.a: 'Oops, bump. All good.'

qa.q: How did laughter carry different messages at two, fifteen and twenty-five?
qa.a: Seema laughed after a bump while checking her mother's reaction and settled when her mother stayed calm. Swati laughed while scared during a scolding, and Amandeep laughed about a bad meeting to cope, until a friend's gentle question reached the hurt underneath.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling when she laughed during the scolding?
qa.a: Fear and embarrassment, as her cracking laugh and stinging eyes show.

qa.q: How could the principal respond when Swati laughs during a scolding?
qa.a: Ask what she is feeling instead of reading the laugh as mockery.

grounding: Laughter that does not mean amusement at two, fifteen and twenty-five: relief after a bump, nervous laughter, and joking through hurt.

passage:
At fifteen, Sunaina left Chinmay's borrowed atlas out in the rain and the pages swelled. Her first urge was to say the balcony door had been stuck. Instead she walked over at lunch. 'I left your atlas outside and it got wet. I'm sorry, that was careless of me. I'll get you a new one this week.' Chinmay's face relaxed, and by the afternoon they were arguing about cricket again.

At twenty-five, Divyansh, who sat next to her at work, sighed loudly over his screen. 'Everyone dumps things on me, and now the report is late and somehow it's all my fault.' Sunaina listened until he ran out of words. 'That sounds like a lot of pressure,' she said. 'What do you want to do about the report?' He mumbled something about sending an apology. 'That sounds sensible. I can proofread it for ten minutes, but I can't take over the analysis. I have my own deadline.' Divyansh sighed again, but he opened a blank email.

qa.q: What did Sunaina offer Chinmay to make up for the atlas?
qa.a: She said she would get him a new one that week.

qa.q: How did Sunaina's response differ when she was at fault and when another person blamed everyone else?
qa.a: At fifteen Sunaina said sorry for leaving the atlas in the rain and offered a new one, and the friends were soon arguing about cricket again. At twenty-five she listened to Divyansh, asked what he wanted to do about the report, and said she could proofread but could not take over the analysis.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling as he sighed over his screen?
qa.a: Overwhelmed and put upon, feeling the late report was unfairly his fault.

qa.q: Why is Sunaina's question about the report useful?
qa.a: It moves Divyansh from complaint toward a next step while she stays kind and firm.

grounding: The same person owns a mistake plainly at fifteen and, at twenty-five, listens with compassion while keeping her limits with someone who blames others.
